note.explanation: Acids react with alkalis or metal oxides to make salt and water, with reactive metals to make salt and hydrogen, and with carbonates to make salt, water and carbon dioxide. Alkalis also react with ammonium salts to release ammonia.
note.checkAnswer: Salt, water and carbon dioxide are formed.
note.simple: Different substances react with acids and bases in different ways, often making a salt and a gas.
note.checkQuestion: What products form when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
note.title: Reactions of Acids and Bases
steps: Identify the type of substance reacting with the acid.
Use the matching products: metal gives salt and hydrogen; carbonate gives salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Write and balance the chemical equation.
note.answer: Acids react with metals, alkalis or metal oxides, and carbonates in characteristic ways. Alkalis also release ammonia from ammonium salts.

mcqs.stem: Which gas is produced when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
rationales: Magnesium is a reactive metal, so it forms a salt and releases hydrogen gas.
Carbon dioxide is produced when an acid reacts with a carbonate, not with magnesium metal.
Ammonia is released when an alkali reacts with an ammonium salt.
Oxygen is not the gas produced in this acid–metal reaction.

mcqs.stem: What products are formed when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
rationales: An acid reacting with an alkali or metal oxide forms salt and water.
An acid reacting with a reactive metal forms salt and hydrogen.
Acids decompose metal carbonates to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Ammonia is released when an alkali reacts with an ammonium salt.

mcqs.stem: Which metal does not evolve hydrogen gas with acids, according to this section?
rationales: Copper is one of the less reactive metals listed as not evolving hydrogen with acids.
Zinc is a reactive metal that forms a salt and hydrogen with acids.
Magnesium is a reactive metal that forms a salt and hydrogen with acids.
Calcium reacts with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas.
An alkali reacting with an ammonium salt releases ammonia gas.
An alkali reacting with an acid forms salt and water.
Zinc reacting with sulfuric acid releases hydrogen gas.
A carbonate reacting with an acid releases carbon dioxide.

mcqs.stem: Which pair reacts to form a salt and water without producing a gas?
rationales: A metal oxide reacts with an acid to form a salt and water.
A reactive metal and an acid produce hydrogen gas as well as a salt.
A metal carbonate and an acid produce carbon dioxide gas as well as salt and water.
An ammonium salt reacting with an alkali releases ammonia gas.

options: Ca(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble in water.
Cu(OH)₂ is an alkali because all hydroxides dissolve in water.
KOH produces carbon dioxide when dissolved in water.
mcqs.stem: Which statement about the bases mentioned in this section is correct?
rationales: The section states that calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble in water.
Copper(II) hydroxide is stated to be insoluble, not an alkali.
Sodium hydroxide is given as an example of an alkali, which is a water-soluble base.
The section does not say that potassium hydroxide produces carbon dioxide in water.

written.text: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?

rubric.why: The products show the characteristic reaction of a reactive metal with an acid.
rubric.description: Identify calcium sulfate and hydrogen as the products.
rubric.how: State that calcium forms calcium sulfate and releases hydrogen gas.

rubric.why: A balanced equation represents the reaction clearly and earns the final-answer mark.
rubric.description: Write the balanced chemical equation.
rubric.how: Write Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂.

modelAnswer: Calcium sulfate and hydrogen gas are formed.

written.text: Which salt is formed when HCl reacts with BaCO₃?

rubric.why: The salt must contain the metal from the carbonate and the negative ion from the acid.
rubric.description: Name the salt formed.
rubric.how: Give barium chloride.

rubric.why: The equation confirms the salt and the products of an acid–carbonate reaction.
rubric.description: Support the answer with the balanced equation.
rubric.how: Write BaCO₃ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

modelAnswer: The salt formed is barium chloride (BaCl₂).

written.text: Is NaHCO₃ a base or an acid? Justify your answer.
written.finalAnswer: NaHCO₃ behaves as a base because it reacts with an acid to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: The response must identify the behaviour asked about.
rubric.description: Identify sodium hydrogen carbonate as behaving as a base in this reaction.
rubric.how: State that NaHCO₃ behaves as a base when it reacts with an acid.

rubric.why: The reaction with an acid is the evidence that justifies the classification.
rubric.description: Explain that it reacts with an acid.
rubric.how: State that it reacts with an acid.

rubric.why: These are characteristic products of an acid–hydrogen carbonate reaction.
rubric.description: Name the other reaction products.
rubric.how: Include water and carbon dioxide among the products.

rubric.why: The balanced example equation demonstrates the stated behaviour.
rubric.description: Give a balanced equation as an example.
rubric.how: Write NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

modelAnswer: NaHCO₃ behaves as a base when it reacts with an acid.
The products are a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

written.text: How does sulphuric acid react with the following compounds? NH₄Cl, NH₄NO₃, MgO, MgCO₃
written.finalAnswer: With MgO it forms MgSO₄ and H₂O; with MgCO₃ it forms MgSO₄, H₂O and CO₂. With ammonium salts, sulphuric acid forms ammonium sulphate and the corresponding acid.

rubric.why: A metal oxide reacts with an acid to form a salt and water.
rubric.description: Give the reaction with magnesium oxide.
rubric.how: Write MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O.

rubric.why: A metal carbonate reacts with an acid to produce carbon dioxide as well as salt and water.
rubric.description: Give the reaction with magnesium carbonate.
rubric.how: Write MgCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

rubric.why: The answer must account for the reaction with ammonium chloride.
rubric.description: State the products for ammonium chloride.
rubric.how: Give ammonium sulphate and hydrogen chloride as products.

rubric.why: The answer must account for the reaction with ammonium nitrate.
rubric.description: State the products for ammonium nitrate.
rubric.how: Give ammonium sulphate and nitric acid as products.

rubric.why: The correct salts are the essential final products of the reactions.
rubric.description: Identify the salts formed.
rubric.how: Name magnesium sulphate for the magnesium compounds and ammonium sulphate for the ammonium salts.

written.text: What happens when a base reacts with a non-metallic oxide. What do you infer about the nature of non-metallic oxide?
written.finalAnswer: A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form a salt and water. Therefore, non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature.

rubric.why: The response must identify the reacting substances in the question.
rubric.description: Describe the reaction between a base and a non-metallic oxide.
rubric.how: State that a base reacts with a non-metallic oxide.

rubric.why: These are the products that describe the reaction.
rubric.description: Name the products.
rubric.how: State that salt and water are formed.

rubric.why: The inference about the oxide's nature is specifically requested.
rubric.description: Infer the nature of non-metallic oxides.
rubric.how: State that non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature.

rubric.why: A correct example supports the explanation and gives the final-answer mark.
rubric.description: Give a suitable example equation.
rubric.how: Write 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.

modelAnswer: A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form a salt and water.
This shows that non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature.

written.text: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water (i) for a short duration (ii) for a long duration?
written.finalAnswer: (i) Lime water turns milky due to insoluble CaCO₃. (ii) On passing excess CO₂, the milkiness disappears because soluble Ca(HCO₃)₂ forms.

rubric.why: The short-duration observation is the first part of the investigation.
rubric.description: State the observation for a short duration.
rubric.how: Say that lime water turns milky.

rubric.why: The insoluble calcium carbonate explains the milkiness.
rubric.description: Identify the precipitate responsible.
rubric.how: Name insoluble calcium carbonate.

rubric.why: The long-duration result occurs because carbon dioxide continues to pass through the mixture.
rubric.description: Describe the condition for the second observation.
rubric.how: State that excess carbon dioxide is passed through.

rubric.why: The second observation differs from the first and must be stated.
rubric.description: State what happens to the milkiness.
rubric.how: Say that the milkiness disappears or the solution clears.

rubric.why: The soluble product explains why the mixture clears.
rubric.description: Name the soluble product formed.
rubric.how: Give calcium hydrogen carbonate, Ca(HCO₃)₂.

modelAnswer: For a short duration: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
The insoluble CaCO₃ makes the lime water turn milky.
For a long duration: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂
The soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate forms, so the milkiness disappears.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask for the products of an acid reacting with a metal, carbonate, alkali or metal oxide. Learn each product pattern.
For reaction questions, write a balanced equation and include state symbols when they are given in your textbook.
For an observation question, state both what is seen and the product that explains it.
In questions about alkalis and ammonium salts, identify ammonia gas as a product.

explain.title: Acids react with alkalis and metal oxides
explain.body: Both reactions produce a salt and water. For example, an acid neutralizes an alkali, while it also reacts with a metal oxide to form salt and water.

explain.title: Acids react with metals and carbonates
explain.body: Reactive metals such as magnesium and zinc react with acids to form salts and release hydrogen gas. Acids react with metal carbonates and hydrogen carbonates to form salts, water and carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Bases and alkalis
explain.body: The textbook defines alkalis as: “alkalis are those bases which are soluble in water.” NaOH and KOH are examples. Calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, while copper(II) hydroxide is insoluble.

explain.title: Alkalis release ammonia
explain.body: An alkali reacts with an ammonium salt to form a salt, water and ammonia gas. Remember that ammonia is different from the hydrogen produced in an acid–metal reaction.

mistakes: Do not confuse the gases: reactive metals with acids produce hydrogen, carbonates with acids produce carbon dioxide, and alkalis with ammonium salts produce ammonia.
Do not forget water when writing the products of an acid–carbonate reaction.
Do not say that all bases are alkalis; an alkali is a base that is soluble in water.
Check the number of atoms on both sides so the equation is balanced.
